newsitem.title: NIGERIA: UN rights envoys call off Nigeria visit - diplomats.
newsitem.headline: UN rights envoys call off Nigeria visit - diplomats.

text.p: A planned visit to Nigeria by two U.N. human rights investigators has been cancelled after the military government refused to allow them access to detainees, diplomatic sources in Lagos said on Wednesday.
"We understand the visit will not happen any more because they could not agree on whom the U.N. rapporteurs should meet," said one senior Western diplomat monitoring the planned visit.
In a statement from the capital Abuja on Wednesday, the Nigerian government said it took every step to ensure the visit and blamed the rapporteurs for the cancellation.
"Government is satisfied that it had put in so much towards the preparation of the mission," said the statement reported by the official News Agency of Nigeria.
"There is much more to the mission that meeting with any particular individual to warrant aborting or postponing it on account of lack of agreement on such minor issues," it added.

Param Cumaraswamy, U.N. special rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers, and Bacre Waly Ndiaye, U.N. rapporteur on extrajudicial, summary or arbitrary executions, had expected to look into the fate of 19 Ogoni youths who are detained over the 1994 murder of four Ogoni chiefs.

They face the death penalty like executed author Ken Saro-Wiwa, who was hanged with eight other Ogoni minority rights activists in 1995 over the same murders after a trial condemned internationally as unfair.

The mission, invited by the government, had been due to visit Nigeria from February 23 to March 5 in time to report back to the U.N. Human Rights Commission, which opens its annual session on March 10.

The investigators had also asked to see Moshood Abiola, the presidential claimant who has been detained on charges of treason since 1994 when he proclaimed himself president in defiance of the military brass.
They had also expected full access to other detainees and dissidents which U.N. sources in Geneva said was the normal terms of reference for such fact-finding missions.
"It seems this was not accepted by the government," one diplomat said.

Local newspapers said an official from the U.N. Human Rights Center, Alan Parra, who had been negotiating in Abuja with Nigerian authorities regarding access, had left after failing to secure guarantees that the team could see detainees.
"All negotiations were unsuccessful," Parra was quoted by the independent Guardian newspaper as saying at Lagos airport on Tuesday night before flying back to Geneva.
In Geneva on Tuesday a U.N. spokeswoman had said that the investigators' visit was unlikely because Nigeria had not agreed to their request for free access to detention centres.
Nigeria will be one of the countries in the dock when the main U.N. human rights forum opens its annual six-week meeting in Geneva on March 10, according to U.N. sources.
